find: The central image is a pond in the garden, where the narrator and his <dfn class="term" data-def="A recurring image, object, or idea that accumulates symbolic meaning across a text.">motif</dfn>-laden toy boat is sailed with his grandfather. The pond functions as a symbol of contained happiness — a still, bounded world the boy shares with the old man, and from which his mother is initially absent.
replace: The central image is the pond in the local park, where the narrator sails a toy motor launch with his grandfather. The boat is the story's key <dfn class="term" data-def="A recurring image, object, or idea that accumulates symbolic meaning across a text.">motif</dfn>. The pond is a symbol of contained happiness — a still, bounded world the boy shares with the old man. When the boat sinks, the outings stop for good.
note: F1: the pond is in the public park ('The pond in our park was circular, exposed, perhaps fifty yards across'), not the garden; the mother is present at the pond.

find: The story's emotional movement is driven by two losses: the grandmother's death before the story opens, and the arrival of Ralph, the mother's new partner, which displaces the grandfather emotionally. Grandfather and boy have formed a unit of mutual consolation; Ralph's presence shatters this. The story climaxes when the grandfather, having grown increasingly withdrawn and silent, poisons himself.
replace: The narrator's father is already dead — his plane went down in the Irish Sea — so the boy and his mother have sold their house and moved in with the grandfather. The grandmother is dead too. Grandfather and boy have formed a unit of mutual consolation, and Ralph, the mother's new partner, shatters it. The grandfather retreats to his garden shed, where he does the chemistry experiments that give the story its title. He finally drinks prussic acid from that shed and dies.
note: F2: the father's death and the grandfather's chemistry shed are the story's founding facts; the lesson omitted both and named the wrong two losses.

find: His suicide by poisoning is never stated explicitly; it is presented through the boy's partial understanding and confirmed only through inference.
replace: He drinks prussic acid from his shed and the verdict is suicide; what stays uncertain is the narrator's private suspicion that his mother drove the old man to it.
note: F3: the suicide is stated (verdict of suicide by prussic acid); the doubt is about the mother's part, not about the fact of the death.

find: Ralph is not a villain — Swift deliberately resists this simplification. He is kind, tries to include the grandfather, and represents the mother's entirely legitimate right to move forward. But his very presence makes the grandfather redundant within the family. The mother is similarly complex: she loves her father and her child, but she also loves Ralph. She cannot be blamed, and yet harm results. This moral complexity is central to Swift's vision.
replace: Ralph is a large, loud, coarse man whom the narrator fears and hates. He does not try to include the grandfather; he takes over the house and pushes the old man out to his shed. The boy is so angry that he plans to throw acid in Ralph's face. The mother is harder to judge: she has lost a husband and wants a new life, but she sides with Ralph against her own father. The narrator half-blames her for the old man's death, and Swift never settles the question. That moral complexity is central to Swift's vision.
note: F4: Ralph is not kind and does not include the grandfather; he is the man the boy fears and hates and plans to attack with acid.

find: The pond and toy boat are the story's central symbol. They represent the private, grief-bound bond between grandfather and grandson — a world of two mourners that Ralph's arrival cannot enter. When the grandfather stops going to the pond, the reader understands he has given up.
replace: The pond in the park and the toy motor launch stand for the bond between grandfather and grandson. When the boat sinks, the outings stop, and the narrator later believes his mother made it happen. The grandfather withdraws to his shed and his chemistry, and the reader understands he has given up.
note: F1/F5: the outings end because the boat sinks, not because the grandfather stops going.

find: data-revision-tip="Cover this and recall: What does the pond represent, and who is excluded from it at first?"
replace: data-revision-tip="Cover this and recall: What does the pond represent, and what brings the outings to an end?"
note: F5: the tip asked an unanswerable question once the pond claim is corrected.

find: As Ralph's presence grows, the grandfather's visits to the pond become less frequent. His withdrawal from the pond signals his emotional withdrawal from life itself.
replace: The boat sinks on one of these outings and they never go back. The grandfather withdraws instead into his shed and his chemistry, and that withdrawal signals his withdrawal from life itself.
note: F5: same correction inside the collapsible.

find: The pond and toy boat are central motifs: they symbolise the private, grief-bound bond between grandfather and narrator, and the grandfather's withdrawal from the pond signals his emotional collapse.
replace: The pond in the park and the toy motor launch are central motifs: they symbolise the bond between grandfather and narrator, and the sinking of the boat marks the end of that shared world.
note: F1/F5: takeaway repeated the pond error.

find: His father was a coalmiiner;
replace: His father was a coalminer;
note: F6: spelling error visible to students.

find: He has died in a pit accident, suffocated when a section of the mine shaft collapsed and trapped him underground.
replace: He has died in a pit accident: a fall of rock came down behind him at the coal face and shut him in. The fall never touched him — he was smothered.
note: F7: Gutenberg text: 'it fell at th' back of 'im. 'E wor under th' face, an' it niver touched 'im. It shut 'im in. It seems 'e wor smothered.' It was not a shaft collapse on to him.

find: At the opening, a ragged bush of chrysanthemums stands at the gate — associated with the house, with endurance, with the ordinary. Elizabeth's daughter brings a sprig into the house and Elizabeth has a complex reaction to their smell — she associates them with significant moments in her past: her wedding, the births of her children, and moments of illness.
replace: At the opening, ragged pink chrysanthemums hang beside the garden path — associated with the house, with endurance, with the ordinary. Elizabeth breaks off a twig and pushes it into her apron-band. Her daughter Annie says they smell beautiful, and Elizabeth answers: 'It was chrysanthemums when I married him, and chrysanthemums when you were born, and the first time they ever brought him home drunk, he'd got brown chrysanthemums in his button-hole.'
note: F8: the third association is Walter's first drunkenness, not illness; Elizabeth, not Annie, brings the flowers in. Gutenberg text verified.

find: appearing at Elizabeth's wedding, the births of her children, and Walter's death
replace: appearing at Elizabeth's wedding, at Annie's birth, at the first time Walter was carried home drunk, and now at his death
note: F8: takeaway repeated the wrong list.

find: A pen-pal scheme run by the school pairs British and Polish teachers; Carla signs up and is paired with Steve, a Polish-heritage teacher. They exchange letters, and through this correspondence Carla begins to reconnect with her Polish identity — the language, the memories, the sense of a self larger than her job.
replace: Carla overhears the head announce that Polish teachers want pen-friends in English schools to practise their English. She asks for an address and writes to Stefan Jeziorny — 'Steve' — a teacher in Poland. She never tells him she works in the kitchen, and he takes her for a teacher. Their letters are mostly about poetry, and through them Carla reconnects with her Polish identity — the language, her mother's songs, a self larger than her job.
note: F9: Carla is not a teacher and is not 'paired' by a scheme; she asks the head for an address. Stefan is a teacher in Poland, not a Polish-heritage teacher at her school, and she hides her job.

find: Steve eventually visits the school. The story's <dfn class="term" data-def="The point of highest tension or revelation in a narrative, from which the story's resolution flows.">climax</dfn> comes when Carla, who has exchanged intimate and equal letters with Steve, finds herself invisible to him within the school's social hierarchy — he does not see her when he looks at the canteen worker. The encounter is humiliating but also clarifying: it exposes the class divide the story has been building towards, and Carla's response is not defeat but a quiet, dignified assertion of her own worth. The story ends with Carla claiming her identity in full — not for Steve, but for herself.
replace: Stefan comes to the school on an exchange, and Carla dreads being found out. The story's <dfn class="term" data-def="The point of highest tension or revelation in a narrative, from which the story's resolution flows.">climax</dfn> comes after Valerie and the other staff mock his accent and his loud tie. Carla walks up to him in her overall. He knows her at once, takes her hand and sings a Polish song from her childhood, and she sings with him. Her job does not matter to him. The prejudice in the story belongs to the English staff, not to Stefan, and Carla ends by claiming her Polish self openly.
note: F10: Stefan does recognise Carla and welcomes her; there is no humiliating non-recognition. The ending is a shared song.

find: When Steve visits the school, he does not recognise Carla as his pen-friend because he sees only a canteen worker, not a person with an interior life equal to his own. This moment crystallises the story's central theme: class prejudice rendering people invisible. Carla's quiet claim of her own worth is the story's emotional resolution.
replace: When Stefan visits, Carla is afraid he will think less of her for working in the kitchen. He does not. He greets her, holds her hand and sings a Polish song with her. The prejudice lies with the English staff, who mock his accent and his tie — not with him. Carla's open claim of her Polish self is the story's emotional resolution.
note: F10: key fact repeated the invented non-recognition.

find: data-revision-tip="Cover this and recall: What does Steve's failure to recognise Carla reveal, and how does Carla respond?"
replace: data-revision-tip="Cover this and recall: What happens when Carla goes up to Stefan, and who shows prejudice in this story?"
note: F10: the tip asked about an event that does not happen.

find: Steve is a Polish-heritage teacher. In the letters, he is warm, curious, equal. In person, in the school, he is subject to the same class assumptions as everyone else: his status as a teacher makes him part of the institution that categorises Carla as invisible. Dunmore does not make Steve simply a villain — he is not malicious, merely unthinking. But that unthinkingness is the point: class prejudice operates invisibly, without intent, which is precisely what makes it so effective.
replace: Stefan Jeziorny is a teacher from Poland who signs himself Steve. In the letters he is warm, curious and equal, and he is exactly the same in person. His tie is wider than normal ties, red with bold green squiggles — to Carla, 'a flag from another country, a better country'. Valerie and the other staff mock his accent and his clothes. Stefan is the one character who refuses to judge anyone by job, dress or accent, which is what makes the staffroom prejudice so visible.
note: F11: Stefan is not part of the institution and is not unthinkingly prejudiced; he is the outsider the staff mock.

find: When Steve visits the school in person, the visual and institutional markers of class reassert themselves. The contrast between the equalised space of the letters and the hierarchical space of the school is the story's central structural irony, and it makes the climactic non-recognition devastating.
replace: Carla expects the school's hierarchy to reassert itself when Stefan arrives, and expects to be exposed as 'only' a kitchen worker. It does not happen: Stefan carries the equality of the letters into the school itself. The prejudice comes from her English colleagues instead, which is the story's real sting.
note: F10: same invented climax.

find: Steve's visible Polish identity (the tie with its bright Polish colours) is something he can display proudly as a teacher; Carla's Polish identity has had to be worn invisibly, on the inside.
replace: The tie is wide, red with bold green squiggles — not Polish colours, just unashamedly his own. Stefan wears his difference openly; Carla has had to keep hers hidden.
note: F12: the tie is 'red with bold green squiggles', not the Polish national colours.

find: The pen-pal format creates an equalised space in which Carla and Steve meet as equals; Steve's failure to recognise Carla on his visit exposes how class hierarchy reasserts itself the moment social roles are visible.
replace: The letters create an equal space in which Carla and Stefan meet as people rather than roles; when he visits he treats her exactly the same way, while her English colleagues mock his accent and his tie.
note: F10: takeaway repeated the invented non-recognition.

find: The son gradually becomes aware that the father has been told the story of Moran, a local man whose son emigrated to America, was drafted into the Korean War, was killed, and whose death brought the family a large insurance payout. The father recounts this story to his son in a way that the son, with growing unease, interprets as more than casual. The son comes to suspect that part of the father's motivation in urging emigration is the prospect of the insurance money if the son should die in Korea.
replace: Luke Moran, a local boy, emigrated to America, was drafted and was killed in Korea. His family were sent home a hero's funeral, ten thousand dollars from the American government and two hundred and fifty dollars a month. While he waits for his exam results, the narrator overhears his father working these sums out with a friend. He understands then that his father is pressing him towards America in the hope that he will be drafted and killed.
note: F13: the son does not piece it together from the father's retellings; he overhears one conversation. The money is US government payment, not private insurance, and the dead boy is named Luke Moran.

find: The story does not confirm this suspicion explicitly. McGahern is too honest a writer to reduce the father to a single motive. But the seed of doubt, once planted, cannot be un-planted — and the son's relationship with his father is permanently altered by the possibility. The story is structured around the gradual, sickening accretion of evidence: small details, the father's tone, the timing of the Moran story, all of which the son assembles into a picture he wishes he could dismiss.
replace: The father never admits this to his son, and McGahern does not reduce him to a single motive: poverty, the loss of the fishing licence and his own war memories all press on him. But the son cannot unhear what he heard. Standing in the dark of the lavatory among the boxes of worms, he knows his youth has ended. At the end he refuses to go, telling his father it will be his own funeral.
note: F13: the revelation is a single overheard conversation, not an accretion of hints; the son's refusal closes the story.

find: The Moran story is the pivot of 'Korea': a local man's son emigrated to America, was drafted to fight in Korea, was killed, and the family received a significant insurance payout. The narrator hears his father recount this story and gradually becomes convinced that the father is partly hoping history will repeat itself — that the son will die in Korea and the insurance money will arrive. This suspicion, never confirmed, is the story's emotional crisis.
replace: Luke Moran, a local boy, was drafted in America and killed in Korea; his family received ten thousand dollars and a monthly payment from the American government. The narrator overhears his father costing this out with a friend and understands that his father wants him to emigrate for the same reason. That overheard conversation, which the father never admits to, is the story's emotional crisis.
note: F13: key fact repeated the wrong mechanism and called the payment insurance.

find: A son returns to post-war Tokyo and shares a tense supper with his father — a meal shadowed by poison, duty, and.
replace: A son returns to post-war Japan for a tense supper with his father, shadowed by poison and duty.
note: F14: the description ends mid-sentence ('duty, and.').

find: Watanabe's death is not condemned — it is described with a kind of reverence, as an act of principle.
replace: The father calls Watanabe 'a man of principle and honour', but when the narrator asks him directly whether the act was a mistake he answers, 'Why, of course. Do you see it otherwise?' — and adds, 'There are other things besides work.'
note: F15: the text has the father condemn the suicide outright. The lesson reversed it.

find: The mother's death from fugu is accidental but sets the tone. Watanabe's murder of his family and suicide is described by the father as understandable — even admirable. This normalisation of death-as-honour within certain cultural codes is central to Ishiguro's exploration of tradition: for the father, to die preserving one's integrity may be preferable to surviving in disgrace.
replace: The mother's death from fugu looks accidental, but the father tells the narrator, 'It's my belief that your mother's death was no accident.' Watanabe killed his wife and his two little girls and then himself; the father respects the man but calls the act a mistake. Ishiguro raises a Western reader's expectation of honour-suicide and then quietly withdraws it, which is what makes the supper so uneasy.
note: F15/F16: the father says the mother's death was no accident, and he condemns Watanabe's act.

find: The father speaks of Watanabe's act with quiet approval, suggesting he views death as an honourable alternative to shame. This is crucial context for reading the ambiguous ending: if the father shares this value, the supper's fish takes on a different weight — one that Ishiguro deliberately refuses to resolve.
replace: The father praises Watanabe as 'a man of principle and honour', but he also says plainly that the suicide was a mistake: 'There are other things besides work.' Note the difference — he respects the man, not the act. That is why the supper stays ambiguous rather than sinister: Ishiguro plants omens and then removes the motive that would make them mean something.
note: F15: key fact repeated the reversal, and a knowledge check was keyed to it.

find: Ishiguro never names the fish served at supper, never shows the father preparing it, and never provides a reaction after the meal ends — because the story ends before any consequences are revealed. The reader accumulates warnings: the mother's death from fugu, Watanabe's murder-suicide, the father's stated admiration for those who act on their principles. These details function like clues that never add up to a definitive answer.
replace: Ishiguro never names the fish — the father says only, 'Just fish' — and the story stops before any consequence could appear. The reader accumulates warnings: the mother's death from fugu, Watanabe's murder-suicide, the father's belief that his wife's death was no accident, and the model battleship that leads him to talk about the pilot's 'final weapon'. These details function like clues that never add up to a definitive answer.
note: F15/F17: the narrator does see his father in the kitchen, and the father never states admiration for principled suicide.

find: The house feels unfamiliar; the garden his mother tended appears uncared for. Even the domestic space signals loss and estrangement.
replace: The house feels unfamiliar: room after room is 'startlingly empty', and his father says it is 'too large for a man to live in alone'. Even the domestic space signals loss and estrangement.
note: F18: there is no neglected garden in the story; the emptied house carries this meaning.

find: The garden, overgrown since the mother's death, symbolises what has been neglected and cannot be restored.
replace: The empty rooms of the house, and the old well the narrator once believed haunted, stand for a family life that has emptied out and cannot be restored.
note: F18: the overgrown garden is invented.

find: Ishiguro also structures the story with careful symmetry: the opening describes the narrator crossing Tokyo at night, uncertain; the close mirrors this uncertainty. The supper that gives the story its title occurs near the end, and the story stops before we see whether anyone rises from the table.
replace: Ishiguro also structures the story with careful symmetry: it opens with a cool paragraph explaining exactly how fugu kills, and it closes with father and son sitting in the dark, waiting for Kikuko to bring the tea. The supper that gives the story its title comes near the end, and the story stops before any consequence could show.
note: F19: the story opens with the fugu paragraph and the drive from the airport on a sunny afternoon; the family do finish the meal and move to the tea-room.

find: Claudette Williams on injustice, voicelessness and dignity in a colonial Caribbean classroom.
replace: Hortense is silenced in a Jamaican classroom for questioning Columbus — and answers back years later in England.
note: F20: half the story takes place in England, and the punishment is for a question, not a false accusation.

find: The story is narrated in the first person by a young girl who is one of the overlooked children sitting at the back of the classroom. The narrator is unjustly punished — struck with a ruler by her teacher Miss Henderson for something she did not do. A more favoured child, sitting at the front, escapes justice while the narrator and others at the back are collectively blamed. The narrator reflects on what it means to be part of the <dfn class="term" data-def="The group of overlooked, marginalised children placed at the back of the classroom, deemed less important or capable than those at the front.">invisible mass</dfn> — those who are seen only when punishment is required, never when recognition or fairness is at stake.
replace: The narrator is Hortense, a Black girl seated at the back of a Jamaican classroom while Lorna Phillips, who is white and wealthy, sits at the front. A school inspector asks about Christopher Columbus arriving in the Caribbean. Instead of the expected answer, Hortense asks what Columbus was doing there anyway, and Miss Henderson strikes her knuckles with a ruler. This is what it means to be part of the <dfn class="term" data-def="The group of overlooked, marginalised children placed at the back of the classroom, deemed less important or capable than those at the front.">invisible mass</dfn> — seen only when punishment is required, never when recognition or fairness is at stake. Afterwards Hortense goes for Lorna, who runs off. Her family then emigrate to England, where she is put in a low stream. She and her friends research Black history for themselves, and when Columbus comes up again in an English classroom she answers with real evidence and leaves the teacher with nothing to say.
note: F21: she is punished for questioning the Columbus story in front of the inspector, not for something she did not do; the story continues in England and ends with her being heard.

find: The narrator is struck with a ruler for something she did not do. What makes this injustice particularly pointed is that it is not accidental or ignorant — Miss Henderson knows who the back-row children are, knows that they will not be believed or defended, and punishes them precisely because their invisibility makes it easy and consequence-free.
replace: Hortense is struck with a ruler for asking a fair question. What makes this injustice particularly pointed is that she is punished for thinking, not for misbehaving — the colonial classroom wants the Columbus story repeated, not examined, and a back-row child who challenges it can be silenced without consequence.
note: F21: same wrong reason for the punishment.

find: The narrator and the other back-row children are denied voice in the most literal sense: they cannot speak in their own defence, cannot protest the punishment, cannot be heard even when they try.
replace: The back-row children are denied voice in the most literal sense: Hortense does speak, and is hit for it. Her question is treated as insolence rather than as thought, and the ending in England matters because it is the moment she is finally listened to.
note: F21: Hortense speaks throughout; the story ends with her being heard.

find: The story insists that her dignity was never Miss Henderson's to remove, even if he tried.
replace: The story insists that her dignity was never Miss Henderson's to remove, even though she tried.
note: F22: Miss Henderson is referred to as 'he'.

find: The Darkness Out There was published in 1984 in the collection Pack of Cards.
replace: The Darkness Out There was first published in 1984 in the collection Corruption and Other Stories, and was later gathered into Pack of Cards: Stories 1978–1986 (1986).
note: F23: Pack of Cards is the 1986 collected volume; the story first appeared in Corruption and Other Stories (Heinemann, 1984).

find: Draw threads across all seven stories, group them by theme, and master the AQA Telling Tales 30-mark essay from.

find: Learning to see these connections across the anthology is the most important preparation you can do for the Modern Texts question, because the AQA exam question will present a theme and ask you to write about how the anthology explores it.

find: Chemistry (the fragile grandmother-mother-son triangle)
replace: Chemistry (the fragile grandfather-mother-son triangle)
note: F26: the grandmother is dead before the story opens; the household is grandfather, mother and son.

find: In Korea (McGahern), a son and his father share a fishing trip that quietly exposes the distance between them — the father's violence and taciturnity, products of war, have left their relationship hollowed out.

find: In Chemistry, the grandfather's death is the event around which the story turns — he walks into the pond and drowns, and the narrator must make sense of this loss alongside the loss of the family's pre-Ralph stability.
replace: In Chemistry, the grandfather's death is the event around which the story turns — he drinks prussic acid from his chemistry shed, and the narrator must make sense of this loss alongside the loss of the family's pre-Ralph stability.
note: F27: the grandfather poisons himself; he does not drown. Lesson 1 of this unit states the correct fact, so the unit contradicted itself.

find: the narrator is punished for something she did not do, within a colonial educational system that denies her the right of reply
replace: Hortense is struck with a ruler for asking why Columbus came to the Caribbean, within a colonial system that wants its story repeated and not examined
note: F21: same wrong reason for the punishment.

find: In Chemistry, the surface stability of the grandmother-mother-son household conceals grief, resentment, and the coming displacement.
replace: In Chemistry, the surface stability of the grandfather-mother-son household conceals grief, resentment, and the coming displacement.
note: F26: same wrong household.

replace: Korea (a son's loss of faith in his father after an overheard conversation)

find: the Modern Texts question presents a single question on the Telling Tales anthology. The question will name a theme and ask how the anthology presents it. You write one essay worth 30 marks plus 4 marks for
replace: the Modern Texts section gives you two Telling Tales questions and you answer one. Each names a story and a theme and asks how writers present that theme in that story 'and in one other story from Telling Tales', so you write about exactly two stories — one chosen for you, one chosen by you. The essay is worth 30 marks plus 4 marks for
note: F25: the paper offers a choice of two questions, each naming one story and requiring a second story.

find: Do not write about each story in turn — that produces a list, not an essay. Instead, plan around your theme: decide on 3-4 points you want to make about how the anthology explores it, then select the most relevant stories as evidence for each point.
replace: The question names one story and asks for one other of your choosing, so plan around those two stories only. Decide on 3-4 points about the theme, and bring both stories into each point rather than writing about one story and then the other.
